sections.markdown:
## C — Drinking, drugs and health: how alcohol impairs driving, what sets BAC, New Jersey BAC limits and crash risk, breath-test refusal, standard drinks, signs of an impaired driver, hosts and designated drivers, drugs and marijuana, and vision, hearing and health
Knowledge domain: why alcohol and drugs make driving dangerous, how blood alcohol concentration is set and measured, the legal limits for adults and drivers under the legal drinking age, what refusing a breath test costs, how police spot an impaired driver, how hosts and designated drivers prevent drunk driving, which medicines and drugs impair driving, and how vision, hearing and health affect fitness to drive.

FACT_ID: sec10-F01 | anchor: A01
Alcohol can make a driver overconfident and unable to think clearly, and even a small amount raises the chance of a crash, including when the driver believes they are under the legal limit. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0116]

FACT_ID: sec10-F02 | anchor: A01
After two, three or four drinks, alcohol starts to impair reaction time, coordination and balance, and it also dulls vision and the ability to judge distance. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0116]

FACT_ID: sec10-F03 | anchor: A01
Only time sobers a person up: the liver burns off about 90 percent of the alcohol and the other 10 percent leaves through breath, urine and sweat, which is why quick sober-up tricks fail. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0116]

FACT_ID: sec10-F04 | anchor: A01
Most alcohol-related crashes involve a single vehicle, yet they often kill or seriously injure several people, including passengers, pedestrians and other drivers. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0116]

FACT_ID: sec10-F05 | anchor: A02
Blood alcohol concentration, or BAC, is the only scientific measure of how much is too much, and a simple breath test reveals it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F06 | anchor: A02
BAC depends on four factors: how much alcohol was consumed, body weight, how quickly the drinks went down, and what food was eaten. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F07 | anchor: A02
New Jersey makes it illegal to drive while impaired by liquor or by narcotic, hallucinogenic or habit-forming drugs, and also to drive with a BAC at or above 0.08 percent. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F08 | anchor: A02
For a driver younger than 21, driving with a BAC of 0.01 percent or higher is illegal and carries severe penalties on top of any DUI penalties. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F09 | anchor: A02
At a BAC slightly above 0.05 percent, the risk of causing a crash doubles. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F10 | anchor: A02
Crash risk is six times as great at a BAC of 0.10 percent and 25 times as great at 0.15 percent. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F11 | anchor: A02
Refusing a breath test is illegal in New Jersey, and penalties include losing driving privileges, referral to an Intoxicated Driver Resource Center (IDRC), fines and an ignition interlock device. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F12 | anchor: A02
A driver who refuses a breath test also owes a violation surcharge, and leaving it unpaid suspends driving privileges indefinitely until it is paid. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F13 | anchor: A02
One and a half ounces of 80-proof whiskey, 12 ounces of beer and 5 ounces of wine each hold about the same half ounce of alcohol. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F14 | anchor: A02
According to the studies the manual cites, beer is what most drivers arrested for drunk driving had been drinking. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F15 | anchor: A02
Food slows how fast alcohol enters the blood, but it cannot prevent a high BAC during steady heavy drinking and it does not make anyone sober. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0117]

FACT_ID: sec10-F16 | anchor: A03
Police are trained to watch for five telltale signs of a drinking driver: speeding, weaving, unusually slow driving, jerky changes of speed and abrupt stops at signs or lights. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec10-F17 | anchor: A03
A good host offers alcohol-free drinks and nourishing food, never pushes drinks or refills, and stops serving alcohol well before the party ends. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec10-F18 | anchor: A03
If a guest has had too much, do not let them drive: suggest a nap or an overnight stay, call the police only as a last resort, and remember that a host can be sued over a guest's drunk-driving crash. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0118]

FACT_ID: sec10-F19 | anchor: A04
New Jersey was the first state to officially launch the Hero Campaign for designated drivers. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec10-F20 | anchor: A04
It is illegal to drive in New Jersey while under the influence of any drug, or while carrying any drug without a valid prescription. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec10-F21 | anchor: A04
Do not take a medicine labeled as possibly causing drowsiness or dizziness before driving; cold pills, tranquilizers and some prescription drugs can affect basic driving skills. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec10-F22 | anchor: A04
Drivers using prescription drugs must show proof of the prescription to police when asked, and a drug that requires a prescription is treated as illegal if the driver has none. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec10-F23 | anchor: A04
After alcohol, marijuana is the drug most often found in drivers involved in crashes. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec10-F24 | anchor: A04
Marijuana can weaken a driver's tracking (staying in the lane), distance judgment, vigilance and ability to divide attention among many tasks. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0119]

FACT_ID: sec10-F25 | anchor: A05
Have your eyes tested every year or two, and every year once you are over age 40. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0120]

Misconceptions: quick sober-up methods and eating do not sober anyone up, only time does; beer is not a weaker choice, a standard beer holds as much alcohol as a shot or a glass of wine; believing you are under the legal limit does not mean alcohol is leaving your driving alone; a legal over-the-counter medicine can still impair driving.
Mnemonics: point-oh-eight for adults, point-oh-one under twenty-one; twice the risk just over point-oh-five, six times at point-one, twenty-five times at point-one-five; the impaired-driver signs as speeding, weaving, slow, jerky and quick stops.
Glossary: BAC means blood alcohol concentration, the share of alcohol in the blood; IDRC means Intoxicated Driver Resource Center; designated driver means the person who stays sober to drive others home; ignition interlock means a device that blocks starting the vehicle after drinking; peripheral vision means side vision.
Dynamic facts: the refusal penalties, surcharges and campaign website can change; confirm them on official New Jersey websites.
